title: Redwood discovery - Aegir Logistics latency & throughput
summary: Discovery focused on p95 latency targets, concurrency, streaming requirements, and token/sec benchmarking for Aegir's real-time routing assistant. Discussed hosted vs dedicated vs private tradeoffs, security needs (SOC2, SSO, KMS), and next steps for benchmarks and pilot.
transcript:
Meeting header: 2026-10-14 15:00 PDT | Duration: 52m | Attendees: Samir Patel (Redwood AE), Jules Romero (Redwood SE), Dana Kim (Aegir Head of ML), Ethan Ross (Platform), Priya Nair (CTO)

Summary: Quick discovery to validate latency p95 targets and throughput requirements for a streaming, real-time routing assistant. Customer wants guidance on whether Hosted meets SLOs or if Dedicated/Private required, and a concrete benchmarking plan.

Topics: p95, concurrency, streaming, token/sec, models (13B vs 70B), quantization, KV cache, security (SOC2, SSO, KMS), rollout plan.

-- Transcript --
[00:00] Samir: Hey everyone, thanks for carving out time. I'm Samir from Redwood, AE on this. With me is Jules, our SE. How's everyone doing?
[00:22] Dana: Good morning, thanks. I'm Dana, head of ML. We've got Ethan and Priya on as well. We're mostly here to figure out if we can hit p95 targets with Redwood hosted or if we need dedicated hardware.
[00:35] Jules: Great. Quick agenda — goals, current infra, target SLOs, then dive into concurrency & streaming. Sound good?
[00:42] Priya: Yep, that's right. Short background — we're building a real-time routing assistant for drivers. Latency is really sensitive since it's in-path for navigation decisions.
[00:56] Ethan: To add, our typical requests are short, 20-80 tokens responses, and we expect bursts during shift changes — up to ~200 concurrent sessions.
[01:08] Samir: Perfect, that's the kind of detail we need. Dana, what's your p95 goal today?
[01:15] Dana: Ideally p95 under 300ms for short responses. For longer streaming answers it's more about token/sec — we want at least 120-150 tokens/sec sustained per model when under expected concurrency.
[01:30] Jules: Ok, couple of clarifications — when you say streaming, do you mean server-sent events for partial tokens, or batching where you return chunks?
[01:40] Dana: SSE, streaming tokens so the driver UI can start rendering quickly.
[01:45] Jules: Good. That works with Redwood's streaming APIs. For p95 <300ms at 200 concurrent streams, we need to understand request size distribution and prompt prefix lengths — those drive KV cache hit rates and effective latency.
[02:04] Ethan: Our average prompt prefix is about 120 tokens (driver history + context) and response length average 40 tokens. Peak QPS ~350.
[02:15] Samir: Noted. Very helpful. From experience, hitting 250-300ms p95 on hosted is feasible for smaller models (13B quantized) with optimized kernels and continuous batching; for 70B models it's usually in the 600ms+ range unless you go dedicated.
[02:34] Priya: We're trying to avoid 70B unless absolutely necessary. Cost is a factor.
[02:39] Samir: Totally. That's where Dedicated shines — predictable latency and throughput at scale, and private deployments if you need network isolation.
[02:49] Dana: How much variability do you typically see between hosted and dedicated for p95 at our profile?
[02:56] Jules: Hosted has multi-tenant variability — we mitigate with autoscaling and routing policies, but p95 can have tail events. Dedicated removes noisy neighbors and lets us pin model variants and kernel selections. For your 200 concurrent streams target, recommended path is run hosted benchmark first; if p95 consistently breaches 350ms we propose a dedicated pool.
[03:18] Ethan: Can you run token/sec benchmarks on our prompt set?
[03:22] Samir: Absolutely. Next step would be for you to share a representative prompt set and traffic profile. We'll run controlled token/sec and p95 latency tests on hosted and share histograms.
[03:35] Dana: Great — we can share that. Timeline?
[03:39] Samir: We can kick off as soon as we get the data; expect initial results in ~5 business days.
[03:46] Jules: On the test side we'll do 3 axes: single-request p95, sustained token/sec throughput at target concurrency, and streaming tail latency at start-of-stream. We'll also test model variants: 13B float32, 13B int8/4-bit, and a 30B family if needed.
[04:06] Dana: A question on KV cache — we heavily rely on context reuse. How do you handle that in hosted?
[04:13] Jules: We maintain per-session KV caches; the runtime supports prefix caching and reuse. Transcription note: sometimes auto transcribed as "K V cash" in other calls, hehe. For you, with long prefixes, cache hit rate is important; if hit rate is high effective latency drops significantly.
[04:32] Priya: Security: SOC2 is required, SSO via SAML, and we need KMS integration for key management. Also, audit logs for model inputs are a must — but we need to ensure we can redact PII before logging.
[04:46] Samir: Redwood is SOC2 compliant, supports SAML SSO, RBAC, and can integrate with customer KMS for private deployments. For hosted, we offer encryption at rest and in transit; for stricter controls we recommend Dedicated or Private where you control keys.
[05:02] Ethan: For hosted, are logs tenant separated?
[05:06] Jules: Yes, logs are per-customer; we can also configure retention and redaction rules. We'll share security docs after the call — we'll attach the SOC2 report and KMS integration guide.
[05:17] Dana: Perfect. On the cost side, how do you estimate unit cost for token/sec vs latency tradeoffs?
[05:24] Samir: There are levers — model size, quantization, batching, prefix caching. We'll provide a cost/perf matrix from the benchmarks. Typically quantized 13B hits a sweet spot for cost and latency here.
[05:38] Priya: Can you do sustained testing for, say, 2 hours to catch warm/cold effects?
[05:44] Jules: Yep; we do short sweeps and a longer soak test to show KV cache warm-up and mem pressure.
[05:50] Ethan: Any limitations for streaming concurrency? Like SSE connections per instance?
[05:55] Jules: There are connection limits per runtime worker but we shard across GPUs. For 200 concurrent SSE streams we'll map to a pool of workers; on hosted we'll auto-route but on dedicated we can size GPU count deterministically.
[06:10] Samir: Also worth mentioning model fallback — if a heavier model's latency spikes, we can route to a cheaper/fast variant automatically to meet SLOs.
[06:20] Dana: That's useful. We need guaranteed p95 during peak shifts.
[06:24] Samir: Understood. We'll design a fallback chain in the experiment.
[06:29] Jules: Quick note on benchmarking methodology — we'll replay your traffic profile with varying concurrencies (50, 100, 150, 200, 300) and measure p50/p95/p99, token/sec, and cold start times. We'll provide raw histograms and aggregated summaries.
[06:46] Ethan: For token/sec, do you measure end-to-end including network?
[06:50] Jules: We'll run tests from both our infra and from your VPC if you want private testing. For hosted external test it's E2E including internet latency; for more apples-to-apples we'll run from a colocated test runner or a customer-controlled agent.
[07:04] Priya: Ok. Can you include cost estimates for a 99th percentile SLO?
[07:09] Samir: We'll include cost modeling for hosted and a committed dedicated configuration. For dedicated we'll give monthly committed cost and estimated per-token unit cost.
[07:19] Dana: Another question — do you support token-level throttling or backpressure?
[07:24] Jules: We have rate-limits and built-in queuing; for streaming we support graceful degradation — e.g., reduce chunk size or fall back to non-streaming short reply when overloaded.
[07:36] Ethan: On instrumentation, we need per-request latency, per-token timing, and tracing to tie to our telemetry.
[07:43] Samir: Redwood exposes per-request traces, per-token telemetry hooks, and integrations with Datadog/Prometheus; we'll share the trace schema.
[07:54] Dana: Cool. Any gotchas around quantization artifacts for our domain (navigation, safety-critical)?
[08:00] Jules: Some edge cases — hallucinations can increase slightly on aggressive quantization; we'll run qualitative evals on your prompt set. If it matters we keep a higher-fidelity variant in the fallback chain.
[08:12] Priya: How do you recommend we start — pilot on hosted or jump to dedicated?
[08:18] Samir: Most customers start hosted to validate functional and perf characteristics quickly, then move to Dedicated when cost/latency requires. Given your 200 concurrent streaming SLOs and strict p95, starting hosted benchmarks is low-friction. If hosted can't meet the p95 consistently, we'll propose a dedicated sizing.
[08:36] Dana: OK. Next practical Q: what data will you need?
[08:40] Jules: Representative prompt set (50-200 prompts), traffic distribution (QPS, concurrency over time), and a checklist of SLOs (p50/p95/p99 targets, token/sec targets).
[08:52] Ethan: We'll get that shared by end of next week.
[08:56] Samir: Great. We'll run the initial suite and come back with: latency histograms, token/sec numbers, cost model, and recommended deployment (hosted vs dedicated).
[09:07] Dana: Also attach SOC2 and KMS docs please.
[09:10] Samir: Yep. We'll upload the security pack.
[09:13] Priya: For timelines, if you run a 2-hour soak test, how long until you share the analysis?
[09:18] Jules: About 2 business days after tests complete to analyze and generate the report.
[09:22] Ethan: One more — do you support custom kernel tuning for our workloads?
[09:26] Jules: We do kernel selection/compilation optimization in the runtime; for Dedicated we can go further with custom tuning and bespoke patches.
[09:34] Dana: Ok, sounds good. Any competitors we should be thinking about?
[09:38] Samir: People often compare us to Anthropic, OpenAI hosted endpoints, and HF inference offerings. We'll include a short note on differences.
[09:46] Priya: On compliance, if we require customer-managed keys, is that only in Private?
[09:51] Jules: KMS with customer keys is supported in Private and some Dedicated configs; hosted with customer-managed keys is limited — we can discuss options.
[10:02] Ethan: Let's talk briefly about metrics to sign off the pilot — what's acceptable?
[10:06] Samir: Proposed acceptance: p95 < 300ms on 13B quantized model at expected concurrency for 85% of test windows; token/sec >120 sustained per session; <5% error rate for streaming. If you need stricter, we'll adjust sizing.
[10:24] Dana: That's reasonable.
[10:28] Samir: Ok, recap of action items and next steps coming up.
[10:32] Priya: Thanks everyone.
[10:36] — end of call notes (transcribed).

Notes about transcription quality: occasional name errors and auto-capitalization; some technical terms auto-transcribed (e.g., "KV cache" => "K V cash").
